claims.text: The starting catalyst is a multi-element automotive alloy in an as-synthesized, nearly equiatomic state.
A low-temperature oxygen plasma treatment at 50–200 W for 1–5 minutes is the proposed intervention.
Including trace NO and H2O during oxygen-plasma treatment will help reproduce relevant transient exhaust conditions.
The treatment can be performed at near-ambient substrate temperature.
Optimized oxygen plasma will generate a thin, ordered, self-limiting oxide layer on the alloy catalyst.
The plasma-generated oxide layer will reorganize the local distribution of metal atoms.
The oxide layer will stabilize the active phase while preserving accessible catalytic sites.
Reactive oxygen species generated by the plasma will induce selective surface oxidation and metal-atom mobility.
Plasma-induced surface restructuring will enhance the dispersion of active metal sites.
Keeping the oxide layer thin will prevent occlusion of active sites.
The thin oxide layer will protect the catalyst against sintering and poisoning during low-temperature transient operation.
The plasma-treated catalyst will have greater low-temperature catalytic activity than the untreated catalyst.
The plasma-treated catalyst will have greater durability under transient conditions containing H2O and NO than the untreated catalyst.
Plasma treatment will reduce degradation over time relative to the untreated catalyst.
The intervention will not increase overall platinum-group-metal consumption.
The untreated catalyst loses activity and durability under transient low-temperature operation because of sintering and other deactivation mechanisms.
The anticipated benefit applies to transient exhaust operation below 300 °C with controlled NO and H2O exposure.
The anticipated benefit may not extend to high-temperature operation or substantially different exhaust compositions.
